question_text: Which of the following architectural principles states that a system should be designed with the minimum set of privileges required for an entity to perform its authorized function?
explanation:
The Principle of Least Privilege dictates that any user, program, or process must possess only the bare minimum access rights and permissions necessary to fulfill its assigned task.

• Option A (Separation of Duties) divides critical tasks among multiple entities to prevent unilateral fraud or error.
• Option B is correct because it explicitly limits privilege levels to the minimum required threshold.
• Option C (Defense in Depth) implements layered redundant controls to protect assets.
• Option D (Fail-Safe Defaults) ensures that access decisions default to denying permission in the event of failure.

question_text: In distributed database systems, what does the CAP theorem state regarding the simultaneous guarantees a distributed data store can provide?
option_a: It can guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance simultaneously.
option_b: It can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance in the presence of network partitions.
option_c: It guarantees that Performance and Durability are always strictly inversely proportional.
option_d: It asserts that eventual consistency requires synchronous replication across all nodes.
explanation:
Brewer's CAP theorem establishes that in the event of a network partition (P), a distributed system must choose between either Consistency (C) — where every read receives the most recent write — or Availability (A) — where every non-failing node returns a non-error response.

• Option A is incorrect because simultaneous satisfaction of all three properties during a partition is mathematically impossible.
• Option B is correct as it accurately captures the fundamental trade-off required under partition conditions.
• Option C is incorrect as it describes general performance latency rather than the CAP theorem.
• Option D is incorrect because eventual consistency relies on asynchronous rather than synchronous propagation.

question_text: What is the worst-case time complexity of standard Quicksort when an unbalanced pivot selection strategy is utilized on an already sorted dataset?
explanation:
When Quicksort repeatedly selects an extreme element (such as always choosing the first or last element) on an already ordered array, the recursive partition degrades into subproblems of size n-1, resulting in O(n^2) quadratic time complexity.

• Option A is incorrect because O(log n) describes the recursive stack depth under balanced partitions.
• Option B is incorrect because O(n log n) represents the average and best-case performance with balanced pivots.
• Option C is correct as unbalanced partition trees lead to n levels of recursion processing linear work.
• Option D is incorrect because comparison-based sorting algorithms cannot execute in O(n) worst-case time.
